title: The Swift That Never Landed
creature: A swift eleven years in the air
summary: Ada works out that the bird outside her window has not touched ground since she was born.

chapters.title: The Bird That Does Not Sit
chapters.text: Ada noticed it because of the wires. There were four wires across the yard behind the flats, and everything sat on them. Pigeons sat on them in a row like a badly made fence. Starlings sat on them and shouted. A collared dove sat on the middle one every afternoon in the same spot and did nothing whatsoever for an hour at a time, which Ada respected. The swifts never sat on them. They came in May and they were gone in August and for those three months they went over the yard at eleven o'clock at night still screaming, in loops, four and five together, at a speed that made the pigeons look like furniture. And in all of it — she watched properly, from the fire escape, for two summers — not one of them ever landed on anything. Not the wires. Not the gutters. Not the aerial, not the flat roof of the bin store, not the one tree. She mentioned it to her mother, who said they must land somewhere, everything lands somewhere. She mentioned it to her teacher, who said it was a good observation and moved on. She mentioned it to Mr Iqbal on the ground floor, who had been a merchant seaman and now had a telescope pointed permanently at nothing in particular, and Mr Iqbal put down his tea and said, "Ah. Well. Now you've asked the right person the right question, which almost never happens, so I'm going to enjoy this."

chapters.title: Eleven Years
chapters.text: What Mr Iqbal told her, over about six weeks, in the wrong order and with a great many diversions, was this. A swift lands to nest. That is the only reason. It builds under an eave or in a gap in a wall, it raises its young, and then it goes, and it does not come down again until the next nest. A young swift leaves the nest and goes into the air and *does not land at all* until it is two, or three, or in some cases four years old. It flies to Africa and it flies back and it does it again, and in between it never once stops. It feeds in the air. It drinks in the air, off the surface of a lake, without stopping. It gathers material for the nest out of the air — bits of seed-fluff and feather that happen to be up there — because it cannot pick anything off the ground. And it sleeps in the air. It goes up at dusk, very high, two thousand metres, and it sleeps up there in the dark going round and round, and it comes down in the morning. "That's not true," said Ada. "It's extremely true," said Mr Iqbal, "and it took people a very long time to believe it, and if you'd like I'll show you where to check, because you should never take a fact off an old man who is enjoying himself." She checked. It was true. It was true in a way that made her cross. She had been alive for eleven years on a planet where this was going on, and nobody had mentioned it. It was not a secret. It was not even difficult. It was in a library book on the second shelf of a public library in a town with a retail park in it, and every adult she had ever met had been walking around not saying anything about it. She put this to Mr Iqbal, with some heat. "Yes," he said, delighted. "Now you have found the actual problem, and the actual problem is not swifts." "What is it, then?" "People are given a small number of facts at school and they assume, quite reasonably, that if there had been better ones, those would have been included." He picked his tea back up. "Nobody hid this from you, Ada. It is simply that the world is a great deal stranger than the timetable has room for. Most people never find that out. The ones who do generally find it out by becoming annoyed about a bird, or a rock, or a number, and it is always an accident, and it is always small." She sat on the fire escape that evening in the warm and did the arithmetic, and the arithmetic is what got her. A swift that has not nested has not landed. If a bird had hatched under an eave the year Ada was born, and had gone into the air that August, and had not yet nested — and some of them do not, for three or four years — then that bird had been flying, continuously, without ever once putting its feet on anything, for as long as Ada had been alive. Every night she had ever slept, it had been awake or asleep in the air. Every single thing she had ever done, it had been flying. She tried to make the thought hold still and it would not. Every meal. Every argument. The whole of Year Three. The fortnight her mother spent in hospital and the fortnight after it. The night the boiler went and they all slept in the front room. Every one of those had happened inside a stretch of time in which something weighing about as much as a bar of chocolate had been continuously airborne, over nine countries and two seas, without once stopping. She could not decide whether that made her feel small or whether it made her feel slightly accompanied, and after about a week she stopped trying to decide and let it be both.

chapters.title: How a Thing Sleeps in the Air
chapters.text: It became, that summer, a slightly unreasonable interest. Her mother's word for it was *fixation*, said fondly in June and less fondly by the third week of July. Ada is prepared to admit this now. She kept a notebook. She wrote down times: first bird of the evening, last bird, direction of the loops. She got a library book that was too old for her and read the parts she could. She annoyed her mother by explaining swift digestion at dinner on four separate occasions. The question that would not leave her alone was the sleeping. She could accept the flying. Flying is what wings are for. But the idea that a creature could be asleep — properly asleep, off, gone — two kilometres up in the dark, and continue to fly, seemed to her to be a much bigger claim than anybody was treating it as. She asked Mr Iqbal how it worked. He was in the yard when she asked, in the deckchair he kept behind the bin store, with the telescope pointed at the same nothing as always. "Nobody entirely knows," he said, with enormous satisfaction. "The current thinking is that half the brain sleeps and the other half keeps an eye on things, and then they swap. Dolphins do something similar. But if you are asking me whether anyone has been up there at two in the morning and watched — no. They have not. There are radar traces and there is a French pilot in 1914 who flew into a lot of them at two thousand metres at night and never got over it, and that is roughly the state of human knowledge." "So it might be something else." "It might be anything at all," said Mr Iqbal. "That is the good news." Ada started going out on the fire escape at eleven, which was permitted, and at two, which was not. She thought about the French pilot for weeks. She looked him up in the end, at the library, on a computer with a sticky keyboard. There was not much. A few lines, repeated in several places, all of them obviously copied from each other. A reconnaissance flight at night in 1914. Two thousand metres over the lines. He had cut the engine to glide, and come down through an enormous number of birds, and in the silence he could hear them all round him, and they were not visible and were not disturbed by him. What got her was the detail about cutting the engine. He had not been looking for anything. He had switched off for some ordinary practical reason, in a war, at night, and in the quiet that followed he had found out something true about the world that nobody on the ground knew — and then had had to land, and had had nobody to tell, and had written it down anyway. She wrote *1914* on the inside cover of the notebook and did not explain it to anybody. She never saw one at two. Of course she didn't; they were two thousand metres up. But she went out anyway and stood in the cold with her head back, and there was the orange sky over the retail park, and the aerial, and the one tree, and nothing. And she knew that they were up there. Directly up there. Above the flats, above the retail park, above the whole ridiculous orange glow of it, going round in slow circles in the actual dark with half of themselves asleep. She has said since that this was the first time in her life she understood that something can be completely true and completely invisible at the same time, and that the two facts have nothing to do with each other. She tested the idea on other things for about a month, which is what you do when you are eleven and have got hold of a good one. The water in the pipes in the wall of her bedroom, going somewhere, all night. The tectonic plate under the retail park, moving at the speed a fingernail grows. Whatever was in the sealed flat on the third floor that nobody had opened since Mrs Kaur died. The fact that on the other side of the world it was Wednesday afternoon and a very large number of people were having an ordinary day she would never hear a single detail of. Some of these worked better than others. Mr Iqbal was given all of them and rated them.

chapters.title: The Gap Above the Window
chapters.text: In the third summer they came back on the eleventh of May, and on the fourteenth one of them landed. Ada was on the fire escape. It came in off the loop, fast and flat the way they do, and instead of pulling up it went straight at the wall of the flats — at the point where the render had come away above her bedroom window, leaving a gap about the width of two fingers — and folded, and went in. She did not move for a long time. There had been a swift nest above her bedroom window and she had not known, and the reason she had not known was that a swift going into a hole does not slow down first. There is no landing. There is a bird at forty miles an hour and then there is no bird. She told Mr Iqbal the next morning and he came up the stairs, which he did not do, and stood in the yard with his head back for a quarter of an hour. "Above the window," he said. "Yes." "Above your window." "Yes." He put his hands in his pockets. "You understand what that means," he said. "That bird has been coming back to that hole every May since before that render came off, probably. They use the same hole. They use it for years. Which means for the whole time you were lying in that bed noticing that they never land — that one was landing about a metre and a half above your head, six times a day, for three months a year." Ada thought about that for the rest of the summer and has thought about it, on and off, for twenty years since. She is at university now, doing something entirely unrelated, and she goes home in May. The render has still not been fixed. She has asked, twice, in writing, that it not be fixed, and has had one letter back from the housing office that did not really engage with the question. She sits on the fire escape at eleven at night when she is home, and the loops go over, and she cannot tell one from another and never could. Somewhere in that noise is a bird that has not touched the ground since April, and will not until next April, and is going to sleep tonight two kilometres above the retail park with half its head switched off. She finds that she thinks about it whenever she is having a difficult week. Not as a comfort exactly. More as a fact she likes having available: that while she is doing whatever she is doing, badly, in a small room, something is up there going round.
